comparison: Both address VEGF-A signaling claims (C9-C15, C67). OpenEval finds evidence SUPPORTED with convergent genetic/pharmacological approaches and positive controls. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, citing insufficient quantitation, lack of demonstration that MO disrupts VEGF signaling, missing information about other vegf genes/isoforms, and inadequate documentation of Shh inhibition degree. Editors emphasized this requires 'strong support' as a key advance.

Both evaluate receptor requirement claims (C16-C22, C82-C86). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED based on expression analysis, morpholino knockdown, and genetic mutants with phenocopy validation. Peer reviewers also find SUPPORTED after revision, initially requesting mutant data to validate morpholinos, which authors provided. Second round noted 'Mutant phenotypes have been used to back up the morpholino data' and manuscript was 'much improved.'

OpenEval R2 includes expression pattern claims (C16, C82-C86) that overlap with peer R9. Both find SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers requested acknowledgment of previously published expression patterns (Pauli et al., 2014) but did not challenge the expression data itself. OpenEval emphasizes thorough genetic characterization while peer review focuses on proper citation of prior work.

Both address specification vs. migration distinction (C23-C24). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, emphasizing normal etv2 expression in receptor-deficient embryos as evidence migration defect is not secondary to specification failure. Peer R12 finds SUPPORTED for C23 (co-expression data), noting it establishes receptor presence from earliest stages and combined with C24 shows receptors expressed during specification but only function in migration.

Both evaluate Apln insufficiency claims (C25-C27). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED based on MO and genetic concordance. Peer R3 addresses broader ligand contribution question including C25-C27 plus C36-C41, finding SUPPORTED after revision clarified relative roles of Apln and Ela. Initially reviewers were confused about whether both ligands guide angioblasts; revision clarified Ela is major ligand with Apln playing minor role.

Both address Ela as primary ligand (C31-C34). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED based on expression timing and genetic loss-of-function. Peer R4 finds SUPPORTED for broader Ela-Aplnr pathway novelty (C5, C31-C35, C63-C66), noting manuscript 'much improved' after revisions and accepting temporal expression data and genetic evidence. Reviewers requested acknowledgment of Pauli et al. 2014 but did not challenge novelty of role in angioblast migration.

Both evaluate genetic interaction and ligand redundancy (C35-C41, C63-C65). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with rigorous dose-dependency analysis and complete phenocopy in double mutants. Peer R3 finds SUPPORTED after revision, noting 'Description of relative roles for Apln and Ela in the migration of angioblasts is now much clearer,' accepting dose-dependency data and interpretation that Ela is major ligand.

OpenEval R6 includes temporal expression claims (C35, C63-C65) that overlap with peer R4's evaluation of Ela-Aplnr pathway. Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes temporal expression differences supporting distinct developmental roles. Peer review accepted temporal expression data as supporting pathway requirement after revisions addressed methodological concerns.

Both address notochord as signal source (C42-C50) and rescue experiments (C51-C52). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, emphasizing correlation between notochord defects, ela expression loss, and migration defects, plus statistical rescue data. Peer R5 finds SUPPORTED, noting 'most of the requested control data have been provided' and manuscript 'much improved.' Genetic analysis in notochord mutants and rescue by Ela overexpression were not specifically challenged.

Both address rescue experiments (C51-C52, C91). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with statistical analysis (chi-square, p<0.001) establishing necessity and sufficiency. Peer R11 finds SUPPORTED for rescue data itself, noting n numbers and statistical tests appropriately provided after revision, though mechanistic interpretation (chemoattraction vs. motogen) remained uncertain in peer evaluation.

OpenEval R8 addresses rescue experiments (C51-C52, C91) that overlap with peer R5's evaluation of necessity and sufficiency. Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes statistical support and critical test of model. Peer review accepted rescue experiments as demonstrating necessity and sufficiency of midline Ela expression without specific challenge.

Both evaluate chemoattraction mechanism (C53-C57, C92-C93). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with quantitative data showing preferential localization (p=0.0001, p=0.0089) and retained motility in receptor-deficient cells arguing against general motility defect. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, stating data 'supported only weakly' based on 'single supplementary figure panel,' needs 'further examples and quantitation,' and 'not compelling.' Alternative interpretation suggested: Ela increased motility rather than chemoattraction. Second round noted 'low numbers' and recommended toning down conclusion.

OpenEval R9 includes quantitative chemoattraction data (C92-C93) that peer R11 addresses. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with statistical significance. Peer R11 finds SUPPORTED for rescue data itself but notes concerns about chemoattraction interpretation were raised separately. Reviewers accepted rescue experiments demonstrated Ela sufficiency to restore migration.

Both evaluate cell autonomy through transplantation (C58-C61). Perfect claim overlap (Jaccard=1.0). Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes well-designed experiments with quantitative data (n=39, 62, 15 angioblasts) and statistical analysis (2-way ANOVA, p<0.001), with reciprocal transplants definitively demonstrating receptor requirement in migrating cells. Peer reviewers did not raise specific concerns about these experiments in either review round.

Both address novel pathway synthesis (C4-C7, C62, C66, C68). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, emphasizing comprehensive experimental evidence and strict requirement distinguishing it from VEGF-A. Peer R4 finds SUPPORTED for Ela-Aplnr pathway novelty (C5, C31-C35, C63-C66) after revisions, noting manuscript 'much improved' and 'most of the reviewers' recommendations have been addressed.' Novelty of role in angioblast migration accepted.

Both address novelty claims (C6-C7, C68-C69). OpenEval finds C69 (therapeutic potential) UNCERTAIN as speculative requiring additional mammalian evidence, while C6-C7, C68 SUPPORTED. Peer R15 finds SUPPORTED for novelty after revisions addressed concerns, noting manuscript 'much improved.' While C69 is speculative, reviewers did not challenge it as appropriate discussion point.

Both address basic developmental process (C1-C2, C75). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as confirmatory context supported by time-lapse imaging. Peer R13 finds SUPPORTED as established background facts, requesting explicit statement about developmental staging to rule out delays, which authors addressed. These descriptive claims about normal development were not challenged.

Both address prior literature citations (C28-C30, C70-C73). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting citations establish precedent for ligand-receptor mismatch and contextualize current findings. Peer R14 finds SUPPORTED, requesting appropriate acknowledgment of prior work (Pauli et al., 2014) but not challenging accuracy of literature citations. These establish background against which novel findings are presented.

Both address therapeutic potential and novelty (C69, C94, C6-C7, C68). OpenEval finds UNCERTAIN for C69/C94 as speculative requiring additional evidence in mammalian systems. Peer R15 finds SUPPORTED for novelty claims after revisions, noting C69 therapeutic potential is speculative but reviewers did not challenge it as appropriate discussion point.

Both address prior literature establishing prevailing model (C3, C70-C73). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting current work challenges this model in zebrafish, highlighting potential species-specific differences. Peer R14 finds SUPPORTED as accurate representation of prior published work providing context. Citations appear appropriate and establish background.

Both address mutant generation and characterization (C78-C81). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as essential methodological information supporting reproducibility. Peer R8 finds SUPPORTED, noting reviewers initially requested mutant analysis to validate morpholinos, and second round explicitly stated 'Mutant phenotypes have been used to back up the morpholino data,' indicating acceptance of mutant generation and characterization.

Both address Shh inhibition validation (C89-C90). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as methodological validation. Peer R10 finds UNCERTAIN, with Reviewer 3 criticizing lack of quantitative data documenting degree of Shh signaling inhibition. While authors showed vegfaa reduction by in situ, reviewers wanted more rigorous quantitative demonstration of Shh pathway inhibition. Editors required 'A reduction in Shh signalling should be demonstrated.'

OpenEval R16 includes staging information (C76) that peer R13 addresses. Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes C76 as essential methodological information for reproducibility. Peer review requested explicit statement about developmental staging to rule out delays (point 1 in second round), which authors addressed.

OpenEval R3 includes C24 (normal etv2 in receptor-deficient embryos) that peer R2 addresses as part of receptor requirement evaluation. Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes this as important control for interpreting migration phenotype. Peer review accepted after revision provided mutant data.

OpenEval R5 includes temporal expression claims (C87-C88) that peer R9 addresses. Both find SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes temporal expression correlates with migration window. Peer review accepted temporal expression patterns as supporting stage-specific ligand functions in revised manuscript.

OpenEval R7 includes C42 (notochord as signal source) that appears in peer R14's literature context evaluation. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of experimental evidence. Peer R14 addresses C42 as citation to prior work, finding SUPPORTED as accurate literature representation.

OpenEval R1 includes C13 (cyclopamine experiment) that peer R14 addresses as part of literature context. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of convergent evidence. Peer R14 finds SUPPORTED as citation but peer R10 separately rates the cyclopamine validation (C89-C90) as UNCERTAIN due to lack of quantitative Shh inhibition data.

OpenEval R9 includes C53 (addressing alternative motility mechanism from prior work) that peer R14 addresses as literature context. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, noting retained motility argues against general motility defect. Peer R14 finds SUPPORTED as accurate citation, though peer R6 separately questions whether chemoattraction vs. motogen interpretation is compelling.

OpenEval R11 includes C4 (synthesis claim) that peer R2 mentions. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of coherent model synthesis. Peer R2 finds SUPPORTED for receptor requirement claims after revision, with C4 accepted as part of overall findings.

OpenEval R11 includes C62 (chemoattraction synthesis) that peer R6 addresses. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as part of comprehensive evidence. Peer R6 finds UNCERTAIN for chemoattraction mechanism, stating data 'not compelling' and suggesting alternative interpretation that Ela increased motility rather than providing directional guidance.
